Two Iberias, 1094

Two maps of the same day, 15 June 1094. On the left, history: the day the real El Cid took Valencia. On the right, the same day at the end of a 94-turn campaign of Nuño Sempere's El Cid wargame, where the exile ended up founding a crowned, three-faith realm on two continents. Drag the handle to swipe between them.

Start here

The real story

Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, called the Campeador and later El Cid, was a Castilian knight exiled by King Alfonso VI in 1081. He spent five years as a commander for the Muslim rulers of Zaragoza, then made himself the dominant power on the eastern coast by collecting tribute from its small Muslim states. On 15 June 1094 he took Valencia after a long siege and ruled it until his death in 1099. Three years later his widow Jimena abandoned the city to the Almoravids.

The peninsula he lived in was split. In the north stood the Christian kingdoms of León–Castile, Aragon, and the Catalan counties. The south was a patchwork of taifas, the Muslim city-states left behind when the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed in 1031. After Alfonso took Toledo in 1085, the taifa kings called in the Almoravids from Morocco, who crossed in 1086, beat Alfonso, and by 1091 had deposed most of the taifa kings themselves.

The game

The wargame starts in June 1081 with the player as Rodrigo on the eve of his exile. An AI narrator runs the world. Each turn the player queues orders: actions, whose outcome the world decides; decrees, which always happen; facts, which the world must accept; and information requests. The narrator then reports what happened and moves the clock on.

This campaign's play followed one idea: rather than carve out a lordship, build a state that could outlive its founder. Its centrepiece became the Charter, a single law engraved on copper plates and mounted on every city gate, naming one land in three languages (Hispania in Latin, al-Andalus in Arabic, Sefarad in Hebrew) and making Christians, Muslims, and Jews equal before its courts.

Taifa
One of the Muslim successor states of the Caliphate of Córdoba.
Parias
Protection money the taifas paid to Christian kings.
Almoravids
A Berber reform movement and empire based in Marrakesh, led by Yusuf ibn Tashfin.
Mesnada
A lord's personal company of knights.
Qa'id
A military commander or governor in a Muslim state's service.
Tizona
The Campeador's sword in legend.

Polities

What the game changed, by 15 June 1094

  • A kingdom instead of a lordship. The historical Cid died lord of one city. In the game his daughter Elvira and foster-son Ramón were crowned at Valencia on 1 November 1093, holding their crown from the Pope and owing homage to no king.
  • No Almoravid Spain. In history the Almoravids ruled everything from Seville to Almería and Murcia by 1094 and held al-Andalus for half a century. In the game their fleet was destroyed off Almería in 1090, Yusuf ibn Tashfin died a prisoner, and his son Abu Bakr was killed in the desert in 1094. Their empire is gone.
  • Iberians in Morocco. The game's realm holds Ceuta, Tangier, and the whole Moroccan coast, and governs Fez, Meknes, and Marrakesh as a joint fief whose revenue mostly goes to Castile. No Christian Iberian power held Moroccan territory for long until Portugal took Ceuta in 1415.
  • Barcelona absorbed. The County of Barcelona joined the realm when its old count abdicated to his son at the coronation. In history, Barcelona merged with Aragon only in 1137.
  • Zaragoza survives as an ally. The last taifa, openly allied and with guaranteed borders. In history it fell to the Almoravids in 1110.
  • Castile smaller but crowned "emperor". Alfonso VI keeps the north and the Tagus, gains Cuenca, and is recognised as Imperator totius Hispaniae, a title he really used. He loses everything south of the Tagus except Mérida. Portugal under Henry of Burgundy is a friendly, separate county. In history Henry only received Portugal around 1095–96, as Alfonso's vassal.
  • The Balearics and the western cities. Ibiza is held directly and Mallorca–Menorca is a vassal protectorate. Lisbon, Santarém, Évora, and Badajoz are Charter cities. In June 1094 the real Lisbon was briefly Castilian, and Badajoz was in the last months of an independent taifa.

The game's chronicle, 1081–1094

1081
  • Accused of skimming the parias he collected at Seville, Rodrigo is banished by Alfonso VI and crosses into Zaragoza with his mesnada, where the sultan al-Mu'tamin takes him into service.
  • A feigned-weakness counter-ambush north of the Segre breaks a raiding force sent from Lleida.

History: also exiled in 1081, and also into Zaragoza's service.

1082
  • A pitched battle on the Ebro against al-Mundhir of Lleida and Count Berenguer Ramon II of Barcelona. Lleida falls in April and is held for Zaragoza with the Campeador as its qa'id.
  • He rebuilds it as a model city: open toll stations, resettlers, an endowed mosque and qadi's court, later a house of learning, a paper press, and crossbow workshops. Alfonso accepts tribute and lets his wife Jimena and their daughters join him.

History: Rodrigo beat the same coalition at Almenar in 1082 but took no city.

1084
  • Tortosa opens its gates on the same terms as Lleida. Al-Mundhir keeps Dénia as Zaragoza's vassal.
1086–87
  • The Almoravids cross the strait, as in history.
  • In 1087 the Campeador's army takes Valencia with Barcelona's knights and Genoese ships, while Zaragoza publicly takes the credit. Seven years ahead of history.
1088
  • Castile is beaten and Toledo besieged for a year. A trial by combat disgraces the Campeador's old enemy García Ordóñez.
  • Cuenca falls to a night assault through its western postern.
1089
  • The Charter is proclaimed: one law for one land in three names. Alicante opens its gates to it.
  • An allied fleet with Barcelona, Genoa, and Pisa burns the Almoravid crossings and yards. Castile and the Ebro principality sign a mutual defence treaty at Toledo.
1090
  • April: the Almoravid fleet is destroyed off Almería. Yusuf ibn Tashfin is pulled from the sea a prisoner, and Almería surrenders the next morning.
  • September: a summit at Valencia collapses and the alliance with Castile breaks.
1091–92
  • Granada, Málaga, Seville, and Córdoba fall in a cascade of opened gates, followed by the western cities. Yusuf dies in captivity and is sent home with full honours.
  • Treaties with the Saharan emirs open the gold trade. A rising of Andalusian merchants delivers Ceuta.
  • All Saints 1092: at Rome, Pope Urban II declares a holy war in Africa under the Campeador's banner, but refuses him a crown.

History: 1091 is when the Almoravids took Seville and Córdoba from their taifa kings.

1093
  • January: the Campeador's gangrenous arm is amputated at the shoulder by physicians working from al-Zahrawi's surgical manual. He survives, one-armed.
  • A Cortes at Valencia swears fealty to his heirs, Elvira and Ramón. Zaragoza expels the Almoravid envoys. Tangier surrenders without a blow.
  • August: peace with Castile. Alfonso is acknowledged as Emperor of all Hispania and receives Cuenca and thirty years of Guadalquivir tolls, in exchange for recognising a sovereign Charter crown.
  • 1 November: Elvira and Ramón are crowned in Valencia cathedral, swearing on the copper plates, with blessings in the cathedral, mosque, and synagogue. Ramón's father abdicates Barcelona to him in the same ceremony. The Campeador hands Tizona to his heir.
1094
  • 2 January: the Campeador dies in Valencia.
  • April to June: a joint fleet of the Charter realm, Aragon, Portugal, Castile, and Norman Sicily lands in Morocco. Abu Bakr abandons Marrakesh and is killed by Masmuda tribesmen. The Almoravid empire is extinguished.

History, 15 June: El Cid takes Valencia.

"Peace for our children, and a realm of law for all its peoples. This is enough." The Campeador's toast at his heirs' coronation, as the narrator wrote it.

How this map was made. 180 strongholds were researched region by region, and each historical holder for June 1094 was checked separately by an adversarial fact-checker (sources are listed per stronghold). Game-world holders come from the narrator's closing report of 15 June 1094. Entries marked inferred fill its silences, mainly the smaller towns of al-Andalus and the Moroccan coast. Each land cell of a 1-arc-minute elevation grid (ETOPO) was assigned to the holder whose stronghold could reach it at least cost, with cost rising with slope and altitude and major cities projecting further. Cells where two holders are within 10% of each other are shown hatched as contested marches. Those cells were then painted onto 13,090 real municipalities and parishes (geoBoundaries; Morocco on a hex grid), so frontiers follow real parish lines rather than straight lines. Treat frontiers as models: 11th-century lordship ran through castles and tribute, not surveyed lines.
